period_summary: Citations concentrated heavily in the 2nd–3rd centuries in apologetic and anti-Jewish contexts, then in 4th–5th century Christological controversies. This reflects the passage's central importance for Christian claims about Jesus's crucifixion and messianic identity.

citations.cited_text: They shall look upon him whom they pierced / And they shall look upon me because they have mocked
citations.text_form_note: Justin's citations vary between 'look upon him' (closer to proto-MT אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר) and 'look upon me' (LXX πρός με ἀνθ᾽ ὧν), sometimes adding 'mocked' (κατωρχήσαντο, LXX reading). Multiple citations show he knew both traditions and possibly conflated them.
citations.theological_use: Justin employs this passage as proof that the prophets foretold Christ's crucifixion by the Jews, arguing the 'piercing' refers to the nails and spear. He uses it polemically against Jewish interlocutors to demonstrate Jesus's messianic identity.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's access to both first-person ('me') and third-person ('him') readings by mid-2nd century indicates multiple Greek text forms were circulating simultaneously in Rome.

citations.cited_text: They shall look upon him whom they pierced
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus's citation reflects the third-person 'him' (αὐτόν) rather than LXX's first-person 'me' (με), aligning with proto-MT and later Christian revisions (Aquila, Theodotion). The Latin version also supports 'ad eum' (toward him).
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses this passage to demonstrate the unity of the two Testaments and to prove that Christ's passion was prophesied. He emphasizes the 'looking upon' as the Jews' eventual recognition of the crucified Messiah.
citations.transmission_implication: Irenaeus's third-person reading suggests that by the late 2nd century in Gaul, a revised Greek text closer to the Hebrew was displacing the older LXX first-person reading in Christian circles.

citations.cited_text: respicient in eum quem confixerunt / they shall look upon him whom they pierced
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Old Latin 'in eum' (upon him) decisively reflects the proto-MT third-person reading rather than LXX's 'in me'. His citation of 'confixerunt' (they pierced) also aligns with דָּקָרוּ against LXX's κατωρχήσαντο (they mocked/insulted).
citations.theological_use: Tertullian deploys this text as irrefutable prophecy of Christ's crucifixion, arguing that the Jews literally pierced Christ and will recognize him at his second coming. He uses it to refute Jewish messianic interpretations.
citations.transmission_implication: The Old Latin tradition in North Africa by c. 200 CE clearly transmitted the proto-MT reading, suggesting early Christian Latin versions were translated from revised Greek texts or directly from Hebrew.

citations.cited_text: They shall look upon me whom they pierced / ὄψονται εἰς ἐμὲ ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν
citations.text_form_note: Origen explicitly cites the first-person 'me' (ἐμέ) and discusses the Hebrew-Greek discrepancy in his textual notes. He uses ἐξεκέντησαν (they pierced through), matching John 19:37 and closer to דָּקָרוּ than LXX's κατωρχήσαντο. He notes Aquila and Theodotion read 'him' (αὐτόν).
citations.theological_use: Origen uses the first-person reading to emphasize God's identification with the pierced Christ, exploring the theological depth of divine suffering. He treats the variant readings as reflecting different aspects of incarnational theology.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's awareness of multiple Greek versions (LXX, Aquila, Theodotion) and his preference for the LXX first-person reading demonstrates scholarly knowledge of textual plurality in 3rd-century Caesarea.

citations.cited_text: aspicient in me quem confixerunt / they shall look upon me whom they pierced
citations.text_form_note: Cyprian's 'in me' represents the LXX first-person pronoun, unusual for Latin North Africa by mid-3rd century. His Old Latin text here preserves an earlier stratum closer to the original LXX against the trend toward MT conformity.
citations.theological_use: Cyprian uses this as a prophetic testimony of Christ's passion, cataloging Old Testament predictions of crucifixion. The first-person 'me' reinforces God's direct statement through the prophet.
citations.transmission_implication: Cyprian's citation shows that older LXX-based Latin translations remained in liturgical and testimonial use in North Africa alongside newer MT-conforming texts, suggesting textual diversity in 3rd-century Latin Christianity.

citations.cited_text: They shall look upon him whom they pierced / ὄψονται πρὸς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius uses the third-person 'him' (ὅν) and cites the reading explicitly from the 'other' Greek versions (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) rather than the LXX. He employs ἐξεκέντησαν (they pierced) matching John 19:37.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius presents this as prophetic proof of Christ's crucifixion and the Jews' eventual conversion. He emphasizes the literal fulfillment in the Gospel of John and the eschatological 'looking upon' at Christ's return.
citations.transmission_implication: By the early 4th century in Caesarea, Christian apologists consciously preferred the revised Greek versions (Aquila/Theodotion) over the LXX for apologetic purposes, reflecting deliberate text-critical choices.

citations.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
citations.cited_text: They shall look upon him whom they pierced / ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν
citations.text_form_note: Chrysostom consistently cites the third-person pronoun 'him' (ὅν) and explicitly notes the Evangelist John's citation of Zechariah. His text matches the standardized Byzantine reading, fully aligned with proto-MT.
citations.theological_use: Chrysostom interprets this as prophecy fulfilled at Calvary but also eschatologically at Christ's second coming when all, including those who pierced him, will see and mourn. He emphasizes the remorse of the piercing generation.
citations.transmission_implication: By the late 4th century in Antioch, the Byzantine ecclesiastical text had fully standardized the third-person reading, eliminating LXX variants from liturgical and homiletic use.

citations.cited_text: aspicient ad me quem confixerunt / they shall look to me whom they have pierced
citations.text_form_note: Jerome's Vulgate 'ad me' appears to render אֵלַי (to me) and אֵת אֲשֶׁר (whom), directly from Hebrew. He notes textual variants in his commentary but translates from MT. His 'confixerunt' (they pierced) reflects דָּקָרוּ exactly.
citations.theological_use: Jerome interprets the first-person 'me' as God speaking about the future crucifixion of Christ, whom Jews pierced. He reconciles 'to me' with 'whom they pierced' christologically: God identifies with the incarnate Son.
citations.transmission_implication: Jerome's direct Hebrew translation established a new Latin standard that superseded Old Latin versions, fixing the proto-MT as authoritative in the West while maintaining the theologically significant first-person pronoun.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history reveals a complex textual evolution from the 2nd to 5th centuries. Early citations (Justin) show awareness of both LXX first-person ('me') and proto-MT third-person ('him') readings, indicating textual fluidity. By the late 2nd century, Christian apologists increasingly preferred readings closer to the Hebrew (Irenaeus, Tertullian), likely influenced by Jewish-Christian debates and the circulation of Aquila's and Theodotion's revisions. The verb also shifted from LXX κατωρχήσαντο (mocked) to ἐξεκέντησαν (pierced), aligning with John 19:37 and Hebrew דָּקָרוּ. Origen represents a scholarly exception, preserving LXX readings while documenting variants. By the 4th century, the third-person reading ('him') became standard in both Greek (Byzantine text) and Latin (Vulgate), though Jerome retained 'ad me' from direct Hebrew translation. This trajectory reflects broader Christian text-critical practice: initial reliance on LXX, followed by revision toward Hebrew under apologetic pressure, culminating in standardized texts that favored proto-MT readings.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers initially used Greek translations that said 'they shall look upon me' (matching the original Hebrew), but by the 3rd century most switched to 'they shall look upon him,' possibly due to debates with Jewish scholars. The passage was crucial for proving Jesus was the Messiah pierced at crucifixion. By the 5th century, the 'him' reading became standard in church Bibles, though Jerome's Latin kept 'to me' from the Hebrew.

notable_variants.reading: ὄψονται εἰς ἐμέ / they shall look upon me (first-person pronoun)
notable_variants.significance: The first-person pronoun preserves the LXX rendering and reflects the Hebrew אֵלַי, theologically significant as God's identification with the pierced Messiah. Its gradual displacement by third-person readings shows Christian text revision under apologetic and exegetical pressures.

notable_variants.reading: ὄψονται πρὸς ὃν / εἰς ὃν / they shall look upon him (third-person pronoun)
notable_variants.significance: The third-person reading reflects Aquila's, Symmachus's, and Theodotion's revisions toward the Hebrew אֵת אֲשֶׁר (relative particle + relative pronoun). Its dominance by the 4th century indicates Christian preference for clarifying the prophetic referent as distinct from God, resolving theological ambiguity.

The LXX verb κατωρχήσαντο (from ὀρχέομαι, to dance/mock) diverges significantly from MT דָּקָרוּ (they pierced). Its virtual disappearance in Christian citations reflects universal adoption of ἐξεκέντησαν (pierced), harmonized with John 19:37 and apologetically stronger.

This verb appears in John 19:37 and represents either a Christian revision or early Greek version closer to Hebrew דָּקָרוּ. Its universal adoption by patristic writers indicates the Gospel citation standardized the Christian textual tradition, overriding the LXX verb entirely.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Gospel of John Standardized Christian Zechariah Text
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most striking finding is that John 19:37's citation of Zechariah 12:10 functionally became the textual standard for all subsequent Christian usage, overriding the LXX's divergent reading (κατωρχήσαντο). The verb ἐξεκέντησαν (pierced) appears universally in patristic citations, demonstrating that New Testament texts exerted retroactive authority on Old Testament transmission in Christian communities. This reveals a hermeneutical circle: the Gospel validated a particular Greek rendering, which then became the 'correct' Old Testament text, effectively creating a Christian textual recension independent of both LXX and MT traditions.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Early Christians changed their Old Testament Bibles to match how the Gospel of John quoted Zechariah, showing that New Testament writings shaped which Old Testament texts became standard in the church.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis captures the broad textual history accurately but contains several specific citation references and claims that need verification, plus some oversimplifications about LXX readings.

flagged_claims.claim: LXX πρός με ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ... κατωρχήσαντο (LXX reading)
flagged_claims.reason: The standard LXX of Zech 12:10 reads ἐπιβλέψονται πρός με ἀνθ' ὧν κατωρχήσαντο. The analysis correctly identifies κατωρχήσαντο but the framing that LXX has 'mocked' is correct; however, the claim that Justin sometimes uses 'look upon him' (third person) needs verification — Justin's citations in Dial. 14, 32, 64, 118 generally have first-person or relate to Christ's two advents, and the 'mixed' characterization may overstate variation.

Irenaeus does cite Zech 12:10 but the specific section reference 4.33.11 should be verified; Zech 12:10 also appears elsewhere in AH (e.g., 4.33.11 mentions 'they pierced' but the precise pronoun form attributed needs checking against the Latin/Greek).

flagged_claims.claim: Tertullian, An Answer to the Jews, ch. 10, 13
flagged_claims.reason: Tertullian cites Zech 12:10 in Adv. Iud. 14 and Adv. Marc. 3.7, not primarily chs. 10 and 13. The chapter references appear inaccurate.

The specific location of Origen's discussion of Zech 12:10 textual variants in Comm. Jo. 10.37 is questionable. Origen discusses this variant in other works (e.g., Contra Celsum, or his Hexaplaric notes), and the claim that he 'explicitly notes Aquila and Theodotion read him' at this specific reference needs verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Cyprian, Testimonies Against the Jews, Book 2.20
flagged_claims.reason: Cyprian's Ad Quirinum (Testimonia) Book 2 cites Zech 12:10, but the specific section number 2.20 should be verified — citations of this verse appear in Test. 2.20 area but exact wording attributed needs checking.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius, Proof of the Gospel, Book 10.8
flagged_claims.reason: Demonstratio Evangelica Book 10 deals with passion prophecies, but the specific section 10.8 for this citation needs verification; Eusebius discusses Zech 12:10 in multiple places.

flagged_claims.claim: Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of John, Homily 85.2
flagged_claims.reason: Chrysostom's Hom. Jo. 85 covers John 19, but whether section 85.2 specifically cites Zech 12:10 with the exact wording attributed requires verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Jerome's Vulgate 'ad me' appears to render אֵלַי (to me) and אֵת אֲשֶׁר (whom), directly from Hebrew
flagged_claims.reason: Jerome's Vulgate actually reads 'aspicient ad me quem confixerunt' — the analysis is correct, but the claim that this reflects direct Hebrew translation oversimplifies; the MT is itself ambiguous and the connection between 'ad me' and 'quem confixerunt' is precisely the textual crux.

The Hexaplaric evidence for Aquila/Theodotion at Zech 12:10 is fragmentary; the standard attribution is that Theodotion has ἐξεκέντησαν (vs. LXX κατωρχήσαντο), but the specific pronoun reading attributed to these revisers needs careful sourcing.
